fatal_errors: The proposed mechanism predicts entropy/disorder-enhanced stability, opposite to the target finding that active diffusion, surface-energy-driven Au/Cu segregation, melting, and evaporation cause instability.

The predicted outcome of fewer defects and greater deformation resistance does not address or reproduce the observed particle reshaping, disappearance of 2–4 nm particles, Au/Cu surface enrichment, and approximately 22% size reduction.
The material composition, sub-10 nm size, initial FCC multi-twinned/icosahedral structure, and PLD synthesis state are unspecified.
The intervention omits in situ vacuum heating and correlated aberration-corrected STEM-EDS observations.
explanation: The response is only broadly aligned with the topic of high-entropy nanoalloys at elevated temperature. Its central hypothesis is contrary to the hidden result: the target shows that these nanoparticles are not protected by sluggish diffusion or entropy stabilization. Instead, surface-energy differences drive non-sluggish Au and Cu diffusion to the surface, with shape-dependent diffusion, melting, evaporation, and loss of structural stability above roughly 673 K. The proposed temperature-only MD comparison and artificial constraints on atomic motion do not cleanly distinguish stress redistribution from surface segregation, compositional effects, or ordinary kinetic suppression. A discriminating test would compare particle geometries and sizes while tracking Au/Cu surface concentration, elemental self-diffusivity, shape evolution, and mass or size loss under the same vacuum-heating schedule. The generic boundary and room-temperature baseline also fail to specify the relevant size, shape, composition, temperature threshold, and vacuum regime.
